newsitem.title: BERMUDA: FIGURE SKATING-KWAN READY FOR REMATCH WITH LIPINSKI.
newsitem.headline: FIGURE SKATING-KWAN READY FOR REMATCH WITH LIPINSKI.

text.p: Women's figure skating world champion Michelle Kwan said she skated like a "scared chicken" at the recent U.S. Nationals and was determined to prove at the prestigious Champions Series Final that she is not washed up at 16.

"At this competition I want to show that I've still got it. This is like a fight. You need to be strong," said Kwan Thursday, as she prepared to defend her Champions Series title on Friday and Saturday against an elite field that includes 14-year-old fellow American Tara Lipinski.

The diminutive Lipinski already grabbed one of Kwan's crowns this year when she won the U.S. National Championship earlier this month in Nashville with some help from a flop-filled long-programme by Kwan.
"Hopefully I killed the scared chicken," Kwan said.
"If I miss a jump now, I won't panic. At nationals I kind of went loony. I doubted the jumps," Kwan admitted.
"I'm feeling more confident here. I think I'm ready for this competition."
Amused by the chicken analogy, but nonetheless warning against a repeat of her recent form, Kwan's coach Frank Carroll joked, "If the scared chicken happens again, she's going to be chicken soup."

Kwan and Lipinski will be skating for the title and $50,000 winner's prize in the event which features the six best performers over the course of the six international competitions that make up the Champions Series.
Also challenging the American duo will be Russia's answer to the U.S. youth movement -- 18-year-old Irina Slutskaya, who took bronze at the 1996 World Championships.
More than the money and a title are at stake here, however. A good showing would also provide a significant psychological advantage going into the World Championship in Switzerland in next month.
"I'm ready to go," said Kwan, who until her loss at the nationals 10 days ago had won nine of the last 10 Olympic-style events she entered over the previous two years.
"When I left Nashville, I was okay because I could start training and get my act back together," she said.
Lipinski appeared unfazed by her new status as the youngest national champion in U.S. history.

At Thursday's practice, the 4-foot-8 (1.42 m), 76-pound (34 kg) dynamo from Sugarland, Texas, exhibited the impressive technical skill that catapulted her onto the podium at three international events this season -- a significant improvement after her 15th place at last year's world's.

Lipinski took just one day off to appear on television interview shows and enjoy her victory before heading right back to the ice in Bloomfield Hills, Michigan, where she trains along with men's world champion Todd Eldredge, who qualified for the men's final.
"There's no grace period where you can walk around with a crown," said their coach Richard Callaghan. "You do that and the crown will fall off.
"Nashville was great for Tara because she performed her work. She knew she had to skate her butt off to make the world team and she ended up winning," added Callaghan.
"That can change around this week and at World's. There are no givens any more."
Kwan and Lipinski skate their do-or-die short programmes Friday night -- Kwan to the Dream of Desdemona and Lipinski to Little Women. The final is set for Saturday.
